name: row-data-gateway
intent: Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it.
problem: SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.
context: Applies when business logic is organised as transaction scripts or thin services over a relational schema whose columns map closely to the fields actually used: the gateway mirrors the table structure, no object/relational impedance mismatch is being managed, and identity maps, units of work and lazy loading are either unnecessary or added deliberately as separate patterns. It also fits generated persistence layers, where the gateway classes are produced from schema metadata during the build.
benefits: All SQL for one table lives in one class: clients call finders and instance methods, so a schema change is edited once and query construction is reviewed once.
The mapping is trivial and mechanical (one column to one field plus simple type conversion), which makes gateways an excellent code-generation target from schema metadata.
Reuse: several transaction scripts share the same finder and CRUD methods instead of each re-deriving the same statements.

Domain objects can stay persistence-ignorant: a script works directly with gateways, or a domain object holds a gateway and delegates its data access to it, so the domain model never learns the schema.
Simple, predictable control flow: one object per row means no proxy, no lazy-loading surprise and no hidden flush - the method called is the statement executed.
tradeoffs: One class per table with hand-written finders is tedious; the pattern only pays off when the classes are generated from metadata or the schema is stable (Fowler calls gateways 'a very good candidate for code generation based on a Metadata Mapping').

Keeping both a domain model and gateways yields three representations of the same data (domain object, gateway, row); unless the gateway mirrors the database structure that is one representation too many.
The gateway is coupled to the schema: renaming a column or changing a type edits the gateway and every client that touches the changed fields.

The pattern provides neither identity map nor unit of work: two finds return two objects for the same row, a later update can silently overwrite an earlier one, and consistency across several gateways is the caller's problem (see Identity Map, Unit of Work, Version Number).
Row-at-a-time granularity costs one object allocation and typically one statement per row: loops over finders produce N+1 round trips, and there is no batching or write coalescing.

Virtual gateways over views or queries make updates harder, and two gateways over the same underlying tables can undo each other's writes; finder placement is a further fork - static finders preclude substituting a different data source, while separate finder objects cost an extra class per table.

participants.responsibility: One instance per row: fields mirror the columns, and instance methods insert, update and delete that row (plus a load/factory step that fills the fields from a result row). It contains data-access logic only - never domain logic.
Locates rows by key or by criteria and returns gateway instances. Implemented either as static finder methods on the gateway or as a separate finder class per table when the data source may vary.
Calls finders, reads and writes gateway fields, invokes insert/update/delete and owns the business logic and the transaction boundary the gateway deliberately lacks.
Supplies the connection, prepared statements and transaction scope in which the gateway executes; the gateway must join the caller's transaction rather than open its own.
Keeps one gateway instance per loaded row so repeated finds return the same object and updates do not fight each other; the pattern does not include it, the surrounding application must add it.
Generates gateway classes and their statements from schema metadata, removing the hand-written class-per-table tedium that is the pattern's main cost.

use_cases: Transaction-script applications (order entry, billing runs, batch imports) where several scripts need the same handful of row-level reads and writes.
CRUD-heavy back-office and admin tooling where a screen edits one row at a time and columns map one-to-one onto form fields.
Legacy or externally owned schemas that must be mirrored rather than reshaped: one gateway per table gives an explicit, reviewable seam between the application and someone else's database.
Generated persistence layers: gateways produced from schema metadata on every build, so the tedious class-per-table work is automated and stays in sync with the schema.
Simple mappings inside an otherwise rich domain model, where a domain object keeps a gateway as its data holder instead of copying field values around.
Reporting and fixture utilities that need reusable, parameterised finders for one table without pulling in a full object/relational mapper.

Laminas\Db\RowGateway and RowGatewayFeature (the official laminas-db implementation) expose one row object with save/delete and can materialize table-query results as row gateways, fitting CRUD screens or transaction scripts that edit individual records.

Zend Framework 1's Zend_Db_Table_Row is a documented legacy row-gateway implementation: table queries return row objects with column access plus save/delete/createRow operations, useful when a simple schema is consumed by row-oriented scripts.

The Go dgw tool generates structs and lightweight Table/Row Data Gateway functions from PostgreSQL metadata, demonstrating the pattern as a code-generation choice when a project wants typed CRUD without a full ORM.
avoid_when: The domain model is rich and the mapping is complex: Data Mapper decouples domain objects from the schema properly, and Active Record is simpler when the mapping is simple.
Only one statement per table is ever needed and no per-row object is wanted: Table Data Gateway (or a single query function) carries less ceremony.

You need identity, change tracking or transactional consistency across several objects: add Unit of Work and Identity Map, or choose a mapper that provides them, rather than hand-rolling them around gateways.
Bulk, set-based processing dominates: per-row gateways turn one UPDATE into thousands of round trips.
The store is not a table-per-object model (document store, key-value, event log): the 'row' metaphor and the column-mirroring fields lose their meaning.
anti_patterns: Gateway classes that accumulate business rules (discounts, validation, workflow): that is Active Record wearing a gateway name, and the mapping layer becomes untestable.
One 'god gateway' for the whole database instead of one class per table: the class stops being a row abstraction and becomes an untamed SQL dump.
A per-row SELECT inside a loop, justified by the claim that 'the gateway hides the SQL'.
Using gateways as an in-memory cache: instances parked in static maps without an Identity Map contract, so stale rows are silently written back.
Returning raw SQL strings, connections or result sets from gateway methods, leaving callers coupled to the very schema the gateway was supposed to encapsulate.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: persistence mechanics in the gateway, business decisions in the transaction script or service.
Single responsibility: one class per table, one instance per row.
Information hiding: SQL, parameters and type conversion never leave the gateway.
Don't repeat yourself: each statement for a table is written once and reused by every client.
Dependency inversion at the seam: clients depend on the finder/gateway interface and receive the connection or data source from outside.
best_practices: Always use parameterised statements - the gateway is the single place where injection can be prevented, so it must not build SQL from caller data.
Keep the gateway free of domain logic; when rules start accumulating in it, promote the class to Active Record or move the rules into a service deliberately.
Put finders in static methods while one data source is enough, and switch to a separate finder object per table as soon as the source must be substitutable.
Thread the caller's connection or transaction through the gateway instead of letting it open its own; only then can several gateways commit atomically.
Pair the gateway with Identity Map and Unit of Work (and Version Number for lost-update detection) when several objects are changed in one transaction.
Generate the gateway classes from schema metadata; hand-writing them is the pattern's main cost and its main source of drift.
Prefer one set-based statement for batch work over looping over per-row methods, and wrap driver exceptions in a persistence-agnostic error type so callers are not bound to the driver.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Row Data Gateway (Data Source Architectural Patterns, ch. 10).
